tagline: Village roads and farm country from Frost’s Derry to Hampstead
intro: The Robert Frost Byway runs 21 miles through southern New Hampshire, using NH 28 and local roads through Derry before turning east toward Hampstead. Visit NH presents its villages, farmsteads and orchards as the rural landscape brought to life in Frost’s writing. It is the literary segment of the combined Robert Frost/Old Stagecoach Byway, a 43-mile route wholly within Rockingham County.

The adjoining Old Stagecoach segment follows NH 121 from Atkinson through Hampstead, Chester and Auburn to Massabesic Lake. That stagecoach route once carried travel between Boston and Concord. The byway council makes this early transportation network part of its interpretation of southern New Hampshire’s rural history.

Frost lived in Derry from 1900 to 1911. His farm produced most of the poems collected in A Boy’s Will and North of Boston. After a later period as a junkyard, the state acquired the property in 1964 and completed its restoration by 1975. The house is a connected farm building with two stories and clapboard siding, built in 1884.
Drive south through Derry village to the farm on Rockingham Road, then follow the local-road portion east to Hampstead. There the Frost segment rejoins NH 121 and the Old Stagecoach Byway.

moments.title: East Derry
moments.text: The First Church in East Derry dates to 1769, with an enlargement made in 1824. Behind it lies the cemetery where many early settlers are buried. This Upper Village is Derry’s oldest settlement, established in 1719 by Scots-Irish Presbyterians. In the nineteenth century it had its own post office and shops. The village center includes the Taylor Library, an 1875 town hall now held by the historical society, and Federal-period houses from the early nineteenth century. Alan Shepard’s childhood home is also here. The village sits on a hill along East Derry Road, approximately two miles east of downtown Derry.

moments.title: Robert Frost Farm
moments.text: The clapboard farmhouse that became a literary landmark was later used as a junkyard. Hundreds of discarded cars filled the field behind the house, which fell into disrepair. New Hampshire acquired it in 1964; restoration was complete by 1975. Most poems in Frost’s first two books were written at this farm. He also wrote a dozen articles for poultry trade journals during his Derry farm years. The family moved to Derry Village in 1909 while he taught at Pinkerton Academy. His yearly repairs to a boundary wall with neighbor Napoleon Guay later became the subject of Mending Wall, written in England.

moments.title: Taylor Mill
moments.text: Taylor Mill’s up-and-down saw uses a waterwheel to drive a mechanized version of a hand saw. The mill on Island Pond Road is a replacement for the original, which had been scrapped before Ernest Ballard bought the land in 1939. Ballard bought a similar dismantled mill in Sandown. He and his wife spent two years assembling it and identifying missing parts, including a waterwheel ordered from Pennsylvania. In 1953, he donated the mill and land to New Hampshire. The waterwheel measures twelve feet across and six feet wide. Ballard’s seventy-one-acre gift became Ballard State Forest, with Ballard Pond above the mill.
